questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Indefinite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
questions.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4}-\frac{1}{4}I \\ \frac{5}{4}I & =\frac{2{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))}{5}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5})(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5}+\frac{3}{5}\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5}+\frac{3}{5}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5})(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5}-\frac{3}{5}\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5}-\frac{3}{5}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5}+\frac{3}{5}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5}+\frac{3}{5}(\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5}-\frac{3}{5}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{5}+\frac{3{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{25}-\frac{9}{25}I \\ \frac{34}{25}I & =\frac{3{e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)-5{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}{25} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{3x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x))}{34}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Definite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}(\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{1}{9}I \\ \frac{10}{9}I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =(-\frac{{e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{10}){|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-\pi /3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3})+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}))}{10}+\frac{{e}^{-0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot 0)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot 0))}{10} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{-\pi /3}}{10}+\frac{3}{10} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}({e}^{-\pi /3}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3{e}^{-3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-3x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-3{e}^{-3x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\int {e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3{e}^{-3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-3x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-3{e}^{-3x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3\int {e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3J \\ I & ={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3(-{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3I) \\ I & ={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-9I \\ 10I & ={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{10}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{2}{5}($
{{field-1}} $)$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by  $I=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-x})\,(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))-\int (-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{2}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-x})\,(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))-\int (\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{2}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{2}I) \\ I & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{4}I \\ \frac{5}{4}I & =-{e}^{-x}(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =(-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(-\frac{{e}^{-\pi /2}}{5}(0-2))-(-\frac{1}{5}(0+2)) \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{-\pi /2}}{5}+\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(1+{e}^{-\pi /2}).\end{aligned}
$$
